comment: Brian (ElevenLabs) VO for Episode 19 (300s): France vs Iraq, Group I, Matchday 2, real kickoff Jun 17 2026 (per canon content/Stories/France-vs-Iraq.md). VERIFIED real facts: Iraq's Zidane Iqbal was born in Manchester (2003) to an Iraqi-Pakistani family and named by his father after the French-Algerian legend Zinedine Zidane; he came through Manchester United's academy (became the first British South Asian to feature for Man Utd's first team, a 2021 Champions League appearance v Young Boys) and now plays in the Netherlands - and here he leads Iraq's midfield against France itself. France: 2018 World Cup winners, 2022 finalists, captain Kylian Mbappe (one of the tournament's all-time top scorers), Michael Olise, Ousmane Dembele, William Saliba, Aurelien Tchouameni. Iraq: striker Aymen Hussein, Ali Al-Hamadi (raised in England). Zinedine Zidane: 1998 World Cup winner for France, the 2006 final headbutt. RULES: Ep18 BEL-EGY recap labelled OUR PREDICTION (we predicted 2-1 Belgium). This ending is OUR PREDICTION (2-0 France). Soccer only - round-neck shirts, a pitch with goals, NO helmets/pads. Lines short - never tempo-stretch.

lines.text: A father in Manchester, during a war back home, named his newborn son after a footballer from another country entirely. He called him Zidane.
Tonight, that boy — now a man — walks out to face the very nation his name came from. France.
Last time, we predicted Belgium would edge Egypt two-one — two cursed crowns. Tonight, a story too perfect for any scriptwriter to dare invent.
Welcome back to WorldCup twenty-six Legends, episode nineteen. France versus Iraq. The champions... and the impossible meeting.
And stay with me — because the boy named after a French legend is about to stand toe to toe with the fastest man in football.
First, the history. And this one is true. Zidane Iqbal was born in Manchester, to an Iraqi-Pakistani family, in the shadow of a war back home.
His father named him after Zinedine Zidane — the French-Algerian genius who won France the World Cup in nineteen ninety-eight.
The boy grew up at Manchester United. He trained in the same building as the greats — and became the first British South Asian ever to play for that famous club.
My dad, he once laughed, set the bar pretty high. Now the son named after a French hero leads Iraq's midfield... against France itself.
And across from him stands everything France is.
France. Champions of the world in twenty-eighteen, finalists in twenty twenty-two — a machine of speed, depth, and ruthless quality.
Kylian Mbappe, the captain. One of the greatest goal-scorers this tournament has ever seen, and still in his prime — frightening.
Beside him, Michael Olise — the Magician — who chose France over three other nations, with Dembele's chaos and Saliba's calm behind him.
A team that wins because it is supposed to win. But Iraq did not cross the world to admire them.
Iraq. A football nation written in the shadow of war and sanctions — and somehow, still here, still standing, still believing.
Zidane Iqbal pulls the strings, calm under any storm. Aymen Hussein leads the line with power, Ali Al-Hamadi running beyond.
They have nothing to lose and a whole country watching who never thought they'd see this night at all.
So here is the duel. France's machine against Iraq's miracle. The fastest man alive... against the boy who carries a legend's name.
Our prediction — built on French class, on Iraqi heart, and on a moment of poetry no script could match. Watch.
Minute thirty-eight. Iqbal collects in midfield, Mbappe bearing down — and the boy named Zidane does what he's done since childhood. Stays calm. Plays the simple pass.
It finds Hussein — he shoots — just wide. France breathe. Iraq believe. The whole stadium exhales at once.
But class, in the end, tells. Olise threads the eye of a needle, and Mbappe is gone before anyone moves. One-nil.
And late, the champions add a second — clinical, inevitable, French. Two-nil.
Two-nil to France, in our story. The scoreline says champions. But the night belonged to a boy named Zidane, who stood on the same grass as his name — and did not flinch.
Do you agree? Comment BLEUS if France are simply too much. Comment IRAQ if Iqbal's night is the story of the round.
And the father who named his son? Legend number nineteen: the Namesake. In the worst of the war, he chose a name from across a border.
He believed a ball could connect even nations that called each other enemies. Tonight, his belief walks out in green. Collect him inside the game.
Which brings us to YOU. At WorldCup twenty-six dot world, pick three of the forty-eight nations — and every goal they score... scores for you.
Free to play. Climb the leaderboard, just for fun. No prizes.
Hit like — send this to the friend who believes football is bigger than borders. And subscribe: the legends are only beginning.
